catalog_quote: The tone-bearing unit in Hausa is the syllable. Hausa has three surface tones. Two are level: Low (L), marked with a grave accent (à and àː); and High (H), left unmarked (a and aː). sweep_summary: Hausa (haus1257) is in the catalog as 'tonal', deciding source Caron 2015 (a tone description). Of 23 title-hits, 4 were read in full: Hunter 1980 (already held by the project and already listed) is the key first-hand stress source and CONFIRMS the classification — an instrumental refutation of Abraham's stress claims, concluding 'there is no need for both tone and stress to describe Hausa' (p. 372); Leben 1996 (newly downloaded, SAL open access) CONFIRMS with 'Hausa has High and Low lexical tones but no phonological stress' (p. 139); Alidou 1995 (KU, image-only, scanned) and Churma 1975 (OSU KB) are prosodic-morphology and tone-representation papers, silent on stress. Schuh 1989's Glottolog title 'verb prosody' is a typo for 'verse prosody: Mutadaarik' (Crossref, same pages), so it, Greenberg 1949 and Schuh 1999 are verse-metre noise. Not obtainable: Leben 1980 LI (JSTOR) and Möhlig 1983 (Buske print) are the only two worth acquiring (medium); Inkelas 1988, Bature 1990, Levin 1979/80, Leben 2003 low; the rest (Ayers 1996 English dissertation, Davis 2008 OHG, Ellis 2009 semantic prosody, Baker & Smith 1976 English) are misattached and irrelevant. Recommendation: keep 'tonal'; promote Hunter 1980 p. 372 (with Leben 1996 p. 139) to the deciding stress quotation. lookups used Crossref/Glottolog/DSpace APIs and direct downloads.

There is no need therefore for both tone and stress to describe Hausa. Furthermore, the "prominence" which occurs behaves linguistically like tone and not like stress.

new_statements.reading: First-hand instrumental study (F0 and duration) of the only classical claim of Hausa word stress (Abraham 1934/1959: H syllables stressed, stress shift in LH words). Duration never changes, only F0, and the F0 effects are general tone-context rules, so Hausa needs no stress feature: prominence is tonal. This is a direct 'no word stress; tone only' statement, consistent with Leben 1996 p. 139 ('Hausa has High and Low lexical tones but no phonological stress').

sources.citation: Hunter, Linda. 1980. Stress in Hausa: an experimental study. Studies in African Linguistics 11(3): 353-374.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: The results of the experiment on stress in Hausa lead to the conclusions that while there are contextually conditioned pronunciation changes which occur in certain grammatical constructions in Hausa, these changes cannot appropriately be described in terms of stress but rather must be considered tonal changes. There is no need therefore for both tone and stress to describe Hausa. Furthermore, the "prominence" which occurs behaves linguistically like tone and not like stress.
sources.locator: abstract p. 353; sec. 4 General Conclusions p. 372
sources.note: Instrumental (F0 + duration) test of Abraham's 1934/1959 claim that High-toned syllables are stressed and that stress shifts in LH nouns/verbs before an initial-H word. Pitch of LH and HL words is affected by the following word's initial tone, but duration is not; the effects are general tone/pitch-realization rules. Conclusion: no stress feature is needed for Hausa; the earlier 'stress' reports (Taylor 1923, Abraham, Pilszczikowa 1968, Wangler 1963, Kraft & Kraft 1973) are reviewed on pp. 353-355 as tone-correlated prominence.

sources.quote: Hausa has High and Low lexical tones but no phonological stress, while English has no lexical tones but quite an intricate system of lexical stress. [...] The main factor governing tone in Hausa borrowings from English is the position of main stress in the English source word [...]. In most cases, English main stress is interpreted as a High prominence peak in Hausa
sources.locator: sec. 1 Introduction, p. 139; sec. 3 p. 143; sec. 9 Conclusions p. 153
sources.note: States flatly that Hausa has no phonological stress; English stress in 335 loanwords is mapped onto Hausa tone via a maximally disyllabic 'tonal foot' (HL or level H), not by a one-to-one stress-to-H substitution.
